ability noun

natural talent

also talent, talented, gifted, natural ability

classical

Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.14: quoniam ingenium ejus nōstī
Traupman 28, 158, 267

ingenium, ingeniī n.

noun, second declension

natural ability, talent, cleverness

Inborn ability, as against what is learned: ingenium beside studium (Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.14) or doctrīna. Talented is ingeniōsus (Traupman 32, 158, 390); in the plural ingenia are talented people: scrīptōrum magna ingenia (Sall. Cat. 8.3).

Other words

  • indolēs, indolis f. — natural gifts, promise

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 26: adulēscentēs bonā indole praeditī (Lewis & Short)

    Inborn character and talents, especially the promise of the young (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Quod tibi plānē deest, mī fīlī, nōn est ingenium sed ambitiō!

    What you plainly lack, my son, is not ability but ambition!Traupman 162

  • dē ejus ērudītiōne quod labōrēs nihil est, quoniam ingenium ejus nōstī, studium ego videō.

    About his education you have nothing to worry about: his ability you know, and his application I can see.Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.14

  • sīc saepe ingenia calamitāte intercidunt

    so talents are often lost through bad luckPhaedr. App. 14.7

See also ability, skill, mind, potential.
